children: 0511 GMT - Investors are repricing sovereign debt from the U.S. to Europe and Japan as they adjust to a world of structurally higher inflation, larger government deficits and higher neutral interest rates, BondBloxx's JoAnne Bianco says in a note. "The story on government debt might be 'higher for a lot longer' instead of just 'higher for longer'," the senior investment strategist says. The continued sell-off in bonds isn't solely about inflation, she says. "Investors are demanding a higher term premium to hold long-dated government bonds" as concerns are growing about persistent fiscal deficits and elevated government borrowing needs. In addition, investors are being asked to absorb significantly more government debt issuance than they were a decade ago--and are demanding higher yields as compensation, she says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0507 GMT - The bond market outlook could get worse before it gets better, Allianz Research analysts say in a note. "While current yield levels look attractive, the negative feedback loop between higher rates and debt sustainability could trigger self-fulfilling prophecies in several countries," they say, pointing to France, Italy, U.K., Japan and the U.S. They estimate temporary yield spikes of up to 70 basis points before central banks would weigh in. "But overall, we consider risks as balanced as any demand side shock would rapidly lower yields." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0506 GMT - Investors are likely face a period of higher yields for longer, Vontobel's Christian Hantel says in note. The global bond sell-off continues on the back of renewed tensions between the U.S. and Iran and rising oil prices as a result, the portfolio manager says. Investors also seem to digest Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech at the Jackson Hole symposium and his more hawkish tone, he says. "As Warsh was very firm on bringing down inflation to the 2% target, he also emphasized that there could be more work to do to ultimately achieve this goal," he says. "So now we are likely to live with higher yields for longer." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0503 GMT - Bitcoin edges up but is struggling to break out of its recent range below the $80,000 mark, as global yields' grim march higher keeps risk-off sentiment intact. Current market conditions aren't looking favorable for crypto: The bond selloff is raising an alarm about debt sustainability, and higher energy prices are fanning inflation worries. All these points to a higher-rate environment that dims the appeal of non-traditional assets. On a positive note, institutional demand for Bitcoin has shown resilience, says Milad Azar at XTB MENA. A sustained streak of ETF inflows could underpin the market, while major buyer Strategy's resumption of Bitcoin purchases after a prolonged pause supports sentiment. Inflation data, central bank meetings and crypto legislation progress in the U.S. will remain on the radar. Bitcoin is up 0.2% at $77,581. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0447 GMT - Australia's GDP growth held up respectably in the June quarter, but its composition doesn't point to a re-accelerating economy, says Sunny Nguyen, Head of Australia Economics at Moody's Analytics. Private investment fell, consumers saved rather than spent, and net trade was positive only because people stopped traveling, Nguyen says in an email. While Moody's base case still has the Reserve Bank of Australia holding rates in September, Nguyen sees risk of a November hike as significantly higher. If the September-quarter trimmed mean inflation is at or above 0.9% on quarter, RBA will have little choice but to move the needle again, she adds.(monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0444 GMT - China's housing sentiment likely improved in August, according to BofA Securities in a research note. A BofA survey showed that 40% of respondents expect prices to rise in Tier 1 cities. "The latest Tier 1 recovery appears more genuine, accompanied by inventory drawdown and a recovery in rental yields," they note. That said, sentiment remains weak in Tier 2 cities and the improvement elsewhere has been volatile, the bank says. Investors are watching for more clues on whether a durable recovery is taking hold across the broader housing market, BofA says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0419 GMT - Asian currencies face headwinds from rising U.S. Treasury yields and oil prices, MUFG Bank's Lloyd Chan says in a research report. "Rising oil prices worsen the terms of trade for net energy importers such as Thailand, the Philippines, India, and Korea, while simultaneously boosting inflation expectations," the senior currency analyst says. Since the Jackson Hole economic policy symposium last Friday, Treasury yields have surged across the curve, Chan notes. Also, Brent crude oil price jumped 4.6% Tuesday to nearly $95 per barrel after renewed strikes between the U.S. and Iran, Chan adds. The dollar edges 0.1% higher to 33.32 baht and rises 0.3% to 62.609 pesos, LSEG data show.(ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0410 GMT - Malaysia's central bank is expected to leave its benchmark policy rate unchanged at 2.75% on Thursday, according to seven economists polled by The Wall Street Journal. Given subdued domestic inflation, mixed sectoral growth momentum and continued volatility in global financial markets, Bank Negara Malaysia is expected to remain cautious and data-dependent, say UOB economists Julia Goh and Jasrine Loke. The central bank is expected to stand pat while monitoring external developments closely, they say in a note. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0332 GMT - South Korea's core inflation could remain in the upper 2% range through 1H 2027, Citigroup's Jin-Wook Kim says. The economist estimates underlying inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, to stay at 2.9% in 3Q, 2.9%-3.0% from 4Q through 1Q 2027, and 2.7% in 2Q 2027. The Bank of Korea is likely to "focus on persistent and broad-based inflationary pressure" in core inflation during its rate-hiking cycle, he notes. Sticky core inflation is driven by time-lagged increases in durable-goods prices and demand-side inflationary pressures amid strong gross domestic income growth, he adds. Citi forecasts further BOK rate hikes in November and February 2027. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0322 GMT - The Singapore dollar consolidates against its U.S. counterpart in the Asian session, but may be weighed by renewed U.S.-Iran conflict that has led to higher crude oil prices. The combination of Brent oil price above $90 per barrel and firmer Fed rate-hike expectations is an "unfavorable mix" for Asia, particularly net oil importers, strategists at OCBC say. "Near term, Asian FX may stay under pressure," the strategists add. The U.S. dollar is little changed at 1.2733 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0258 GMT - Indonesia headline and core inflation could still rise further in the coming months, driven by higher input and logistics costs, rebounding energy prices and potential El Nino-related food supply disruptions, Maybank's Brian Lee and Chua Hak Bin say in a note. However, the analysts reckon muted consumer demand could limit the increase. They keep their Indonesia inflation forecasts at 3.5% for 2026 and 3% for 2027. Bank Indonesia is expected to keep its policy rate at 5.75% through the year-end, with a stable rupiah and easing portfolio outflows reducing pressure for further tightening, they add. Elevated inflation and global uncertainty should limit room for near-term easing, while supply-side price pressures are unlikely to warrant higher rates, as policy rates are a demand-side tool, Maybank says. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0255 GMT - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand could raise rates further, but its tightening cycle may be shallow, Capital Economics' Abhijit Surya says in commentary. "The RBNZ hiked rates as expected, but tempered expectations for further tightening," the senior APAC economist says. The RBNZ's "messaging sounded a bit less hawkish than before," the economist says, comparing today's statement with the July statement. Overall, Capital Economics is "comfortable" with its forecast that the RBNZ's official cash rate will peak at 3.25% in 1H 2027, compared with markets' pricing in terminal rate of 3.75% by end-2027, Surya adds. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)
